title: Under Berlin
subtitle: The Berlin Tunnel, George Blake, and the Cold War's Greatest Intelligence Gamble
description: In 1955, American and British intelligence tunneled beneath the Berlin border to tap Soviet military cables, capturing a river of secret conversations. Yet before the first shovel struck earth, MI6 officer George Blake had already betrayed the operation to the KGB. For eleven months, Moscow allowed the wiretap to continue, transforming a daring engineering feat into a labyrinth of counterintelligence. Was the tunnel permitted to run solely to protect a valuable double agent, or did the Kremlin use it to feed the West curated disinformation? Drawing on declassified CIA histories, Soviet archives, and memoirs from both sides of the Iron Curtain, this narrative reconstructs the audacious dig, the staged discovery at Altglienicke, and Blake’s eventual reckoning at the Old Bailey. It is a story not just of espionage tradecraft and subterranean engineering, but of the profound uncertainty that defined the Cold War, where every intercepted word carried the weight of calculated silence and enduring doubt.

editorReview.text: This biography of the Berlin spy tunnel is a model of disciplined historical reconstruction. It resists sensationalism, grounding its core argument—that the operation's ultimate value was frustratingly indeterminate—in a meticulous assembly of declassified records rather than narrative imposition. The chronological structure is admirably faithful to its source material, and insights like its analysis of the 'quality of silence' in intercepted traffic are genuinely illuminating.
